The district health team came to the government school in their small town for a day of talks, boys and girls in separate rooms. Afterwards, at the chai stall, Naveen was loud about it.
"All this 'consent' stuff. If a girl says no, she just wants you to try harder."
Saurabh put his glass down. "Did you listen at all? The nurse said no means no. And quiet or unsure isn't a yes either."
"Relax, it was a joke."
"It's not funny if someone believes it."
Naveen shrugged, but he stopped grinning. Saurabh added, "She also said anyone can go to the health centre with questions, privately. About infections, about protection, whatever. Nobody tells your parents' friends."
Naveen didn't answer. On the walk home, though, he asked where exactly the health centre was.

qa.q: Where did the boys talk after the health talks?
qa.a: They talked at the chai stall.

qa.q: What does Naveen asking where the health centre was suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Naveen was more curious and unsure than his loud jokes showed, and maybe a bit embarrassed to ask openly.

qa.q: How could Saurabh keep supporting his friend?
qa.a: Saurabh could keep calmly correcting myths about "no" and encourage Naveen to take real questions to the health centre privately.

qa.q: If you were a girl hearing Naveen's first comment, how would you feel?
qa.a: You might feel unsafe and disrespected, because the joke treats a girl's refusal as something to push past.

grounding: Shows a teen challenging a peer's myth about consent and pointing to confidential sexual-health information.

passage:
In Valencia, Pablo and his girlfriend Lucía were watching a film on her sofa. They'd been kissing, and then she pulled back a little and said, "I don't want to go further. Not yet."
Pablo felt his face get hot, and for a second he wanted to ask why. Instead he said, "Okay. Thanks for telling me." He meant it. They finished the film holding hands.
On Monday, Lars asked him in the corridor what had happened, grinning. Pablo said, "Nothing you need to know. And if she says not yet, it's not yet."
Lars laughed, but later, walking home, he admitted he'd never been sure what counted as a yes. Pablo told him what the school nurse said in the sex-ed class: ask, listen, and a yes can change to no at any time.

qa.q: What did Lucía say when she pulled back?
qa.a: "I don't want to go further. Not yet."

qa.q: What was Pablo feeling when Lucía said not yet?
qa.a: Pablo felt embarrassed and briefly disappointed, but chose to respect her and felt sincere about thanking her.

qa.q: Why was Pablo's answer to Lars a good one?
qa.a: He kept Lucía's privacy and made clear that her "not yet" was final, which shows respect instead of bragging.

qa.q: How might Lucía feel about Pablo's response on the sofa?
qa.a: Lucía probably felt safe and respected, and more able to trust him because her boundary didn't cause a fight.

grounding: Illustrates a teen respecting a partner's no and passing on accurate consent information to a friend.

The biology teacher at Chinmay's school ran a Friday session with an anonymous question box. This week she pulled out Tarun's slip, though nobody knew it was his: "If someone said yes before, does that mean yes the next time?"
"No," she said. "Consent is every time, for every thing, and it can be taken back."
Next slip: "My cousin says you can't get an infection the first time. True?"
Chinmay sat up; his cousin had told him exactly that. "Not true," she said. "Infections don't count how many times. Condoms help reduce both infections and pregnancy. If you have questions about your own health, the school nurse or a doctor can talk to you privately."
Chinmay glanced at Tarun, who was writing something in the back of his notebook. At the bell, Chinmay said quietly, "Glad somebody asked that." Tarun went red and nodded.

qa.q: What did the teacher say about consent given before?
qa.a: Consent is every time, for every thing, and it can be taken back.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay sit up at the second question?
qa.a: Chinmay felt surprised and alarmed, because his own cousin had told him the same myth.

qa.q: How does the anonymous box help teens learn this topic?
qa.a: It lets students ask embarrassing or personal questions without being identified, so myths come out and get corrected.

qa.q: What is it like for Tarun when Chinmay says he was glad someone asked?
qa.a: Tarun is embarrassed, going red, but probably relieved that his question helped instead of being mocked.

grounding: Shows a class correcting myths about consent and infection risk through anonymous questions.

At first I thought it was love. Aman texted every hour. He wanted to know where I was, who I was with. It felt nice to be missed.
Then it became passwords. "If you've got nothing to hide, why not?" When I spent Saturday at Zeenat's, he sent forty messages and said I was choosing her over him. I apologised, even though I hadn't done anything.
Zeenat was the one who said it out loud. "Sunaina, you check your phone like you're scared of it."
That sentence stayed with me all night. I realised I was scared. I told my mother the next day, all of it. She didn't say "I told you so". She sat with me while I ended it and changed my passwords.
Looking back, love didn't feel like being watched.

qa.a: He sent forty messages.

qa.q: What steps helped Sunaina get out of the controlling relationship?

Counsellor's note: Hemant, Class 12. By Nazia (school counsellor).
Hemant came in upset that his girlfriend "isn't respecting him". When I asked what he meant, he said she won't share her location with him anymore and she went to a cousin's wedding without telling him every detail.
He sees his checking as caring. "What if something happens to her?"
I asked him how he'd feel if she tracked him and asked for a report on every friend he met. He said, "Like I was in jail," then went quiet.
We talked about the difference between caring and control: asking versus demanding, trusting versus checking. He admitted he feels anxious when he can't see where she is, and that it's his anxiety to manage, not hers.
Plan: weekly sessions for four weeks, focusing on his worry. With his permission, I've let his parents know he's seeing me.

qa.q: What did Hemant's girlfriend stop sharing with him?
qa.a: She stopped sharing her location with him.

qa.q: What does Hemant going quiet after saying "like I was in jail" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Hemant felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, starting to see his checking from her side.

qa.q: What would you advise Hemant as he works on this?
qa.a: Keep meeting the counsellor, notice the anxious urge to check and choose to trust or talk openly, instead of demanding reports.

qa.q: How might Hemant's girlfriend have experienced his checking?
qa.a: She may have felt watched and pressured, which is probably why she stopped sharing her location.

grounding: Shows a counsellor helping a teen tell caring apart from control in his own relationship.

Nandini is on the school trip to Shimla till Friday, with boys and girls from both sections. Last year I'd have been texting her every ten minutes asking who she was sitting with. I actually felt that urge today, like an itch.
But I keep thinking of my cousin's boyfriend, who wouldn't let her go to college functions and checked her phone. She cried at Diwali and nobody could fix it.

When she's back we're going for momos. I trust her. And honestly, it feels lighter this way.
Baljeet

At Nani's funeral I didn't cry. Everyone else did. Aunties kept hugging me and I just stood there, feeling like a statue, and then feeling guilty for not crying.
Three weeks later I went into her room to find a pen. Her sewing machine was still open, with blue thread on it, the blouse she'd been stitching for me half-done. And then I couldn't stop. I sat on the floor for an hour.
Parveen came over that evening. She didn't say "she's in a better place". She just sat next to me and asked, "What was she like when she was annoyed?" And I laughed, because Nani used to scold the pressure cooker.
I finished the blouse myself last month, badly. I wear it anyway. I'm Madhuri, and I think grief doesn't come on time.

qa.a: Blue thread, and the blouse she'd been stitching, half-done.

qa.a: Madhuri felt numb, like a statue, and guilty for not crying when everyone else did.

Nandini has been very quiet this week. She usually argues with me about everything. Today she put her head down in the free period. When I asked quietly, she said her dog, Bruno, died on Sunday. He was fourteen, older than her.

Diary, Shreya here. Today was the thirteenth-day prayer for Nana. The house was full of people and incense.
In the afternoon my cousin Hemant and I hid on the terrace and started laughing about how Nana used to fall asleep during cricket and then insist he'd been watching. We laughed so hard. Then I felt terrible. Is it wrong to laugh when he's gone?
Mami found us. I thought she'd scold us. She sat down and said, "He'd want you laughing about him. That's how he stays."
So Hemant and I asked if we could plant a hibiscus by the gate, the red kind Nana always picked for his puja. We did it before sunset. My hands were muddy and I cried a bit.
It feels a little easier tonight.

On Sunday mornings Lakshmi took a book up to the terrace of their small-town house and read for two hours. She loved it: the pigeons, the neighbours' radio, nobody asking anything. She came down calm.
Then her best friend Kiran moved to Chennai. For a few weeks, Lakshmi kept her Sunday reading. But the rest of the week felt different. She ate lunch alone, came home, looked at her phone, waited for Kiran's texts, and felt heavy. The terrace hours were still nice. The other hours weren't.
One evening she realised the difference: on Sundays she chose to be alone. The rest of the week she just was alone.
So she joined the library's Thursday story club. Two girls there loved the same author. She still kept her Sundays for herself.

qa.a: She read on the terrace of their small-town house.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel during the rest of the week after Kiran moved?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt lonely and heavy, waiting for Kiran's texts.

qa.q: Which choice helped Lakshmi, and why?
qa.a: Joining the library's Thursday story club helped, because it tackled the lonely weekdays while she still kept her chosen Sunday solitude.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel on hearing about Lakshmi's story club?
qa.a: Kiran might feel relieved and happy that Lakshmi wasn't sitting alone every day after the move.

grounding: Illustrates a teen telling chosen solitude apart from painful isolation and acting on it.

Fatima's family moved to Toronto in September. By October she was eating lunch every day in the school library.
"I like it," she told her mother. "It's quiet." And some days that was true: she'd read, draw, and feel fine.
But on Fridays, she could hear the noise from the cafeteria, and she'd sit with her sandwich and feel her throat go tight. She started skipping lunch entirely and saying she wasn't hungry.
One day Dalia, from her maths class, came into the library looking for a book. "Wait, you're in here every day? We have a table where people talk about anime. You could come."
Fatima hesitated, then went on Friday. It was loud and awkward and nice. Now she goes Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and keeps the library for the other two days.

She found her in her room with headphones on. "Not hungry?"

Last year I was sleeping about five hours a night. I'd start maths at 10 p.m. because that's when I finally felt awake, then watch "just one" video, and wake up at 6:30 for the school bus feeling like I'd been hit.
I blamed myself for being lazy. Then my friend Gurpreet said her sister, a nurse, had told her teenagers' body clocks actually shift later. That made me feel less stupid, but it didn't fix the bus.
So I tried a few things. I moved maths to 5 p.m. I kept my phone in the living room after 10. On Sundays I didn't sleep till noon, just an hour extra, so Monday wasn't a disaster.
It took about two weeks. Now I'm mostly fine. I'm Yamini, and I still hate 6:30. But I'm not a zombie anymore.

qa.q: What time did Yamini move maths to?
qa.a: Yamini moved maths to 5 p.m.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel on hearing that teenagers' body clocks shift later?
qa.a: Yamini felt relieved and less stupid, no longer blaming laziness.

qa.q: Which of Yamini's changes seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Moving hard study earlier and keeping the phone out after 10, because it works with the late body clock without losing sleep to scrolling.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see Yamini's change?
qa.a: Gurpreet might feel glad that sharing what her sister said helped a friend stop blaming herself.

grounding: Shows a teen understanding a shifted body clock and adjusting study times and phone use.

Lokesh's diary. Today behind the sports shed, Kashish pulled out a vape pen that smelled like mango. "Try, it's not even smoking. It's just flavour."

My father, Ramesh, runs a pharmacy. From when I was little, everyone said I'd do science and take over. I'm Chetan, the only son.

Last month I got a call from someone saying he was from a shopping site. He said I'd been charged twice for my headphones and he'd refund it. "I'm sending a request on UPI. Just accept and enter your PIN to receive the money."
I actually had my thumb on the screen. Then I remembered what my friend Jomon had shown me after his sister nearly got cheated: you never need a PIN to receive money. A PIN is only for sending.
I said I'd call back and hung up. My hands were shaking. I showed the request to my father. He checked with the bank's official number, which said they'd never call like that, and he reported the number.
I'm Kiran, and now I read every UPI screen twice, especially the word "pay".

qa.q: What did the caller say he would do?
qa.a: He said he'd refund the double charge by sending a request on UPI.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after hanging up?
qa.a: Kiran felt shaken and scared, with shaking hands, realising how close it had been.

qa.q: Why was showing the request to Kiran's father the right step?
qa.a: He could verify with the bank's official number and report the fraud, rather than Kiran handling it alone.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel if he learned his tip had helped?
qa.a: Jomon would probably feel glad and proud that his sister's close call protected his friend.

grounding: Shows a teen spotting a UPI refund scam and involving a parent to verify and report it.

Class 9 life-skills note. Yogesh, maths teacher.
This month the class tracked their own pocket money for three weeks, then we discussed patterns. I asked them not to share amounts, only what they noticed.
Aadhya's notebook was the most honest. She'd written every item: bus, a pen, snacks. When she added it up, snacks from the school gate were more than everything else together. She was surprised and a little embarrassed. "They're so small each time," she said.

qa.a: Aadhya felt surprised and a little embarrassed, since each purchase had seemed so small.

qa.a: He pointed her to her parents and a bank official instead of giving personal money advice himself.

qa.q: How might Aadhya's classmates see her findings?
qa.a: They might feel curious to check their own small spends, since hers surprised her so much.

Two days before the municipal election, Neelam's grandfather, Ramesh, got a message on the family group: "The new flyover was built only by Party A. Party B blocked it for years!" He was about to forward it to his 200-member community group.
"Wait, Dadu," Neelam said. "Where's it from?"
"Everyone is sharing it."

Dadu frowned. "So it's half true, half nonsense."
"More nonsense, I think."
He didn't forward it. Instead, he typed in the family group: "Check before sending, it's election time."

qa.q: What does Dadu's frown at the website suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Dadu felt surprised and uneasy, realising he'd nearly spread a misleading claim.

qa.q: What was the key step Neelam took, and why?
qa.a: Checking an official source before sharing, because popularity doesn't make a claim true, especially near an election.

qa.q: How might the 200-member group have been affected if Dadu had forwarded it?
qa.a: Many people could have believed a false story about the parties just before voting.

grounding: Illustrates a teen checking a political claim against an official source under time pressure.

Alka had only seen elections on the news, all shouting. Here it was a queue under a tree, an old man with a newspaper, a volunteer helping an elderly woman.
